analysis.one_liner: Bars pollution discharge permits for shared Great Lakes waters unless every bordering state agrees.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let any Great Lakes state block a shared pollution discharge permit, never left a House subcommittee and died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed the Clean Water Act so that no government agency or state could issue a permit to discharge pollutants into a Great Lake shared by two or more states unless every state bordering that water agreed. A state could only agree after giving local residents notice and a chance to comment. The goal was to stop one state from approving pollution that flows into waters its neighbors also depend on. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live around the Great Lakes, drink from them, fish in them, and recreate on them. Under the Clean Water Act, a discharge permit issued by one state or by the EPA generally governs a waterway; this bill would have added a veto: any state bordering a shared Great Lake could refuse to concur, and residents near the water would get notice and a comment period before a permit was approved. That means no single state could sign off on pollution that ends up in water its neighbors share.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Great Lakes residents and local communities

how_it_helps.text: Before any permit to discharge pollutants into a shared Great Lake could issue, every state bordering that body of water would have to agree, so no single state could greenlight pollution of a lake its neighbors share.
A state could agree to a permit only after giving local notice and an opportunity for public comment, giving residents near the affected waters a say before pollution is allowed.

analysis.who_pays: Facilities that discharge pollutants into shared Great Lakes waters — factories, power plants, and wastewater treatment systems — which would have faced an extra layer of state review and, in some cases, denial or tougher conditions on their permits. Consumers could see some of those compliance costs passed through in prices or water bills.

drawbacks.text: Requiring every Great Lakes state touching a shared body of water to concur before a permit issues could slow or block routine permit renewals, since a single state could hold up a discharge permit even when the other states agree.
The bill applies only to shared waters, so discharges into waters lying entirely within one state would face no additional review, leaving a gap in coverage that polluters could exploit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was stronger, more accountable protection of a shared natural resource that tens of millions of people drink from, swim in, and fish in, with public notice and comment built in at every step. The cost fell on polluting facilities, which would have faced an additional layer of review and possibly tougher permit conditions, and the public could have seen somewhat slower permitting for dischargers. The bill was a single new permit condition rather than a sweeping regulatory overhaul, so its cost was modest and its benefit concentrated on the health of a lake system that no single state could protect alone.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House committee and then to a subcommittee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 3, 2007, with 13 original sponsors, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where it stayed.
No further action was taken before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, so the bill never received a committee vote or a vote on the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that discharge pollutants into the Great Lakes are better off, because the bill's added state-by-state review of permits never took effect. Residents around the lakes gained nothing from its death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Industrial dischargers into the Great Lakes

for.name: Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 13 original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 27 House Democrats and 1 House Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, a bipartisan group drawn largely from Great Lakes states.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took it up; it was passed to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee and no hearing, markup, or vote followed.

against.name: Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment
against.role: Subcommittee of referral, House Transportation and Infrastructure
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from August 4, 2007 until the Congress ended without acting on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 29 sponsors and cosponsors were 27 Democrats and 1 Republican, largely from Great Lakes states, and no one is recorded opposing it because it never came to a vote.

industries.industry: Industrial and wastewater dischargers into the Great Lakes
industries.note: Facilities that discharge pollutants into shared Great Lakes waters would have needed the agreement of every bordering state to keep or obtain a discharge permit, adding a veto point and likely tougher conditions. The practical cost is tighter limits on what they can release into the lakes that residents use for drinking water, fishing, and recreation.
